article.overview: A subsurface acoustic sensor is an instrument placed beneath the lunar surface, in a backfilled hole, a borehole or a drill string, to detect ground-borne vibrations. The Moon has no atmosphere to carry sound, so the signals of interest are elastic waves that travel through the regolith and bedrock; in this article "acoustic" is used in that sense. The catalogue name does not describe one standard instrument, and no flown or operating payload with this exact name was identified in the sources accessed. The article therefore covers three related approaches that have been proposed or tested: buried seismometers, fibre-optic distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) and seismic-while-drilling. None of them has been confirmed operating on the Moon, and their status is set out in each example.
article.description:
A subsurface acoustic sensor converts ground vibrations into a recorded electrical or optical signal, usually with a precise time reference, so that the arrival times, frequencies and amplitudes of seismic waves can be analysed. The sensing element may be a geophone or an optical seismometer buried in the regolith, a length of optical fibre whose backscattered light is disturbed by strain, or a drill-borne source and receiver arrangement. Each approach couples to the ground differently, and each records either at a point or along a line.

Lunar regolith is a low-density, porous layer that scatters and reverberates seismic energy. Placing the sensing element below its upper layer is therefore a central design consideration, because it reduces surface noise and the scattering of signals that would otherwise obscure distant or small events [1][2].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a subsurface sensor is to record ground vibrations with less contamination from the surface than a surface-mounted instrument would receive. The sources accessed describe three main scientific aims. First, buried seismometers are proposed for a Lunar Geophysical Network, a mission identified by the Planetary Decadal Survey, to investigate the Moon's internal structure, crustal thickness, mantle composition and the frequency of moonquakes [1][2]. Second, fibre-optic sensing has been studied as a way to detect distant earthquakes in simulated lunar regolith, and the authors suggest it may be useful where noise limits conventional sensing [3]. Third, seismic-while-drilling uses energy from the drill bit to characterise the drilled section with vertical seismic profiles, which could support subsurface stratigraphy studies during drilling [4]. These applications are proposals or laboratory results. None is a confirmed lunar measurement.
article.operating_principle:
The buried seismometer described in the sources combines a geophone with a laser interferometer. It is described as a novel combination of a geophone and a laser interferometer that enables detection of sub-micron-scale motions [2]. The interferometric readout is reported to increase displacement resolution by orders of magnitude over capacitive measurements while maintaining tilt tolerance [1]. The sensor is described as tilt-insensitive over 180 degrees and as self-calibrating for tilt, which matters because a buried instrument cannot be levelled after installation [1].

Burial uses a gas-jet process. Compressed gas is fed through a hose inside a tube that ends in a cone with holes for gas jets. The gas lofts regolith through the annular space between the tube and the borehole wall, and once the gas flow stops the loose soil flows back in to cover the sensor [1][2].

A distributed acoustic sensing system sends light pulses along an optical fibre and analyses the light scattered back along its length. Strain on the fibre changes the returned signal, which can be converted into a vibration record along the cable. This description of the interrogation principle is general background and is not taken from the sources accessed; the 2025 study used a DAS interrogator reading single-mode fibre [3].

In seismic-while-drilling, energy from the drill bit is used as the seismic source, and the resulting signals are processed into vertical seismic profiles of the drilled section [4].
article.scientific_importance: The Moon's interior cannot be read directly from its surface, and seismic waves are among the few ways to probe it. Apollo deployed a long-lived seismometer network on the Moon from 1969, which showed that lunar seismology can be carried out over long periods [1]. Buried instruments add a specific advantage: the low-density surface layer traps and scatters seismic energy, so a sensor below it can record signals that would otherwise be lost in reverberations [1][2]. Fibre-optic and drill-based approaches could extend this capability by providing long lines of sensing or seismic information gathered during drilling [3][4]. The scientific value of any of these approaches depends on demonstrating sensitivity, coupling and operation in real lunar conditions, which has not yet been shown.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a subsurface acoustic sensor. Each example below is a different architecture at a different stage of development. Values are quoted only where a source states them, and each value is labelled as a measured result, a design target, a plan or not publicly specified.

examples.name: Buried Silicon Audio seismometer with Honeybee Robotics burial system
examples.type: Proposed Lunar Geophysical Network instrument with a burial system; prototype development stage; not flown.
examples.description:
The example combines a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) Silicon Audio seismometer, which the team plans to redesign into a Lunar Geophysical Network (LGN) sensor, with a gas-jet burial system from Honeybee Robotics [1][2]. The COTS device was originally developed for seismic monitoring in support of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty, and the team reports a dynamic range of 183 dB for it [1]. The poster gives a bandwidth of 0.005 Hz to 400 Hz for the Silicon Audio sensor [1]. For the LGN version, the target noise floor is 1×10⁻⁹ m/s²/√Hz with a modest reduction in bandwidth; this is a design goal, not a measured performance [1][2]. Three-axis operation is planned by stacking single-axis units inside a probe [1].

The poster states that the design preserves sensor size and mass, but it gives no mass, dimensions or power values for the sensor itself. It says that the interferometric readout keeps the required power low [1].

The burial target is 50 cm depth into compacted lunar regolith simulant at 90 per cent or greater relative density, in vacuum [1]. Burial tests have used a 50 mm diameter probe sized to accommodate one axis of the sensor [1]. A TRL 4 breadboard of the burial system, developed earlier for a NASA-funded Heat Flow Probe, reached a depth of about 2 m in 1.9 g/cc NU-LHT-2M simulant within two minutes [1]. In vacuum and lunar-gravity tests in a Zero-g Corp aircraft, one gram of gas was reported to loft up to 6000 grams of JSC-1a simulant [1]. The poster also refers to a system mass of 1 kg as a design aim for remote robotic deployment; the sources do not state whether this covers the sensor, the burial hardware or both [1].

The team plans to test the LGN prototype to demonstrate TRL 6 [1]. This is a plan, not an achieved level. Field stations in Alaska and Greenland were established to compare the COTS sensor with terrestrial standards [1]. The Silicon Audio sensor is reported as funded under the NASA DALI and ICEE2 programmes [1]. The sensor was also baselined on the Lunar Environment Monitoring Station (LEMS), a concept that the 2019 poster described with a nominal two-year duration [2]. NASA's August 2026 update says LEMS hardware is complete, that it carries two seismometers, and that it has not been deployed [5].

No image is included for this example. No direct image asset URL could be verified for the sensor or the burial system, so the article relies on text and source references.

examples.name: Distributed acoustic sensing on buried or surface fibre (laboratory simulation)
examples.description:
A distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) system uses a single-mode optical fibre read out by an interrogator to record vibrations along the cable. In a 2025 study, the fibre was tested in a 10 m open-bottom wooden box filled with lunar regolith simulant and deployed indoors. The fibre was buried at several depths, a surface-deployed case was used for comparison, and signals from four regional and local earthquakes were recorded [3]. The abstract does not state the simulant product, the interrogator model, the channel count or spacing, the sampling rate or the burial depths; these would require the full text [3].

The authors report that attenuation of surface-deployed fibre relative to buried fibre was relatively high in active-source experiments, but that this attenuation was not consistently observed in earthquake signals. Burial depth was not highly correlated with attenuation of earthquake signals [3]. Indoor deployment kept atmospheric noise minimal [3]. The result therefore describes a controlled laboratory setting and is not a lunar measurement. No mass, dimensions or power are publicly specified for a lunar DAS system in the sources accessed.

examples.name: Seismic-while-drilling with the drill bit as the seismic source (laboratory tests)
examples.type: Drilling-based seismic method; laboratory tests; not flown.
examples.description:
Seismic-while-drilling (SWD) is a method used on Earth to support drilling for oil, gas and geothermal exploration. Energy from the drill bit is used to characterise the drilled section through vertical seismic profiles [4]. A 2015 paper adapts the method to lunar drilling. Its validation was a laboratory test made within a European Space Agency project completed in 2009, using a simulator of a complete remote system and a planetary drill prototype [4]. The abstract does not report the sensors, the regolith simulant or any quantitative results [4].

SWD therefore characterises a drilling operation rather than providing a standalone sensor. It has not been demonstrated on the Moon [4]. A 2012 MOONBIT study is referred to in related literature as a drill-bit seismic source, but its full text was not accessible during this research, so its details are not used here.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Not publicly specified for any of the three examples in the sources accessed. The only physical value given for the buried seismometer is the 50 mm diameter of the burial test probe, which was sized for one axis of the sensor [1].
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Example 1 refers to a 1 kg system design aim [1]. No mass is stated for the Silicon Audio sensor, a lunar DAS system or a seismic-while-drilling system in the sources accessed.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The poster states that the interferometric readout keeps the required power low, but gives no power figure [1]. The sources accessed give no power figure for the DAS or seismic-while-drilling examples.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen:
A subsurface sensor must survive lunar vacuum, large day-night temperature swings and radiation, and it must couple to a regolith that behaves very differently from terrestrial ground. The surface regolith has a density of about 1200 to 1300 kg/m³ and a porosity near 60 per cent. Within the top 50 cm the density rises to roughly 1900 kg/m³ with a porosity near 40 per cent. The powdered surface layer has P-wave velocities below 100 m/s, and the velocity falls to around 50 m/s within the top metre [1]. These properties trap and scatter seismic energy, which is why burial depth matters [1].

Thermal stress from a lander's daily expansion and contraction creates noise at many frequencies, so a robotically deployed seismometer is intended to sit less than 1 m from its spacecraft, with burial reducing the coupling of that noise [2]. In vacuum, very little gas is needed for burial: the poster describes a few grams as sufficient [1]. Operationally, the sensor must be levelled or tilt-tolerant, thermally protected, and connected to power and data. Specific thermal-survival and lifetime values for a lunar subsurface sensor are not publicly specified in the sources accessed.
article.limitations: A subsurface sensor records a local signal. A single point or line of sensing does not locate events on its own, and a network is needed for that. The burial process itself must be verified on the Moon, not only in simulant. The Silicon Audio performance figures are for a COTS device and a target LGN redesign [1][2]. The burial system is at TRL 4 in the sources accessed [1]. The DAS study is a laboratory simulation with indoor conditions and four earthquakes [3]. Seismic-while-drilling depends on drilling activity and is not a standalone sensor [4]. Simulant behaviour may not match lunar regolith in grain shape, cohesion, moisture or layering; this is a general engineering consideration and not a result from the sources.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: This payload class is delivered as part of a lander or surface experiment package rather than as a separate spacecraft. Its transportation and deployment depend on the architecture.
transportation_process: Integrate the sensor and burial system with the lander or experiment package on Earth.
Launch the package and transfer it towards the Moon.
Land the package on the lunar surface, keeping the seismic sensor away from the lander's thermally noisy structure where possible [2].
Excavate a vertical hole with pressurised gas, lower the instrument into it and allow loose regolith to flow back over it [1][2].
Connect power, thermal control and data interfaces, as the chosen architecture requires.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: For the buried seismometer, the proposed method is robotic burial by gas jet. The gas could come from a small dedicated tank or from residual propulsion gas on the lander [1]. The team's review describes robotic deployment of a seismometer less than 1 m from its spacecraft, with burial about 1 m below the low-density layer to reduce noise from the lander and from scattering [2]. For DAS, the fibre could be laid on the surface or buried; the 2025 study suggests surface-laid fibre may be a practical option in noise-limited settings, but this is a laboratory inference [3]. For seismic-while-drilling, the drill is the active element and the sensors would need to be integrated with the drilling system; the sources accessed do not describe that integration [4].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The NASA-funded Heat Flow Probe burial breadboard is the basis of the burial system in Example 1 [1]. The LEMS concept, which the Silicon Audio seismometer was baselined on, has been completed as hardware but not yet deployed. NASA states that it will remain in a Goddard clean room until it is assigned to an Artemis mission [5]. No subsurface acoustic sensor from this catalogue class has been confirmed deployed on the Moon in the sources accessed.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander, rover or spacecraft has been verified as compatible with any of these examples. The interface data needed for that assessment, including mass, dimensions, mounting, landing loads, power, data and thermal interfaces, are not published for these sensors in the sources accessed.

article.historical_significance: The idea of a seismic network on the Moon has a long history. Apollo deployed a long-lived seismometer network from 1969 [1]. The Planetary Decadal Survey identifies a New Frontiers Lunar Geophysical Network mission as a priority, and the Silicon Audio seismometer and Honeybee burial system were developed as a concept for that mission [1][2]. The concept evolved into LEMS, which NASA describes as complete in hardware and awaiting assignment to an Artemis mission [5]. A 2015 seismic-while-drilling study [4] and a 2025 fibre-optic laboratory study [3] represent alternative approaches to lunar subsurface seismology. In the sources accessed, no payload in this class has yet returned a lunar subsurface record.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The catalogue entry "Subsurface acoustic sensor" does not define a single instrument, so the three examples are not interchangeable and their figures must not be combined. None of the examples is flown or confirmed operating on the Moon. The Silicon Audio performance figures, the noise-floor target, the 50 cm burial target and the TRL 6 plan come from a 2019 poster and a related NASA technical document, and may not match a current design. The NTRS technical document is undated in the text retrieved. The DAS result is a laboratory simulation, and the full text was not read for simulant, interrogator and channel details. The seismic-while-drilling evidence rests on an abstract that gives no quantitative results. The MOONBIT source could not be read in full. The LEMS status comes from a 2026 NASA article and does not describe the seismometer's performance. No direct image asset URLs were verified for any example, so the article contains no images. No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility has been verified, and no lunar landing site is recommended, as instructed.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image URLs were included because no direct image asset URL could be verified for this payload class.

data_quality_notes: No flown or operating payload with the exact name 'Subsurface acoustic sensor' was identified in the sources accessed. The article interprets the catalogue entry as a class covering three approaches: buried seismometers, fibre-optic distributed acoustic sensing and seismic-while-drilling.

No image is included. No direct image asset URL was verified for the Silicon Audio seismometer, the Honeybee burial system, the DAS study or the seismic-while-drilling work. The NTRS PDFs contain figures, but no standalone verified asset URL was identified, so image_url values were not invented.

The Silicon Audio performance figures (183 dB dynamic range, 0.005 Hz to 400 Hz bandwidth, 180-degree tilt insensitivity), the LGN noise-floor target of 1x10^-9 m/s^2/sqrt(Hz), the 50 cm burial target and the TRL 6 plan are taken from a 2019 SSA poster (NTRS 20190018069) and a related NASA technical document (NTRS 20190032450). They are design targets, claims or plans, not measured flight performance.
The NTRS 20190032450 document was read from its PDF text, but its publication date is not confirmed in the text retrieved.

The '1 kg' value in Example 1 is described in the poster as a design aim for remote robotic deployment; the source does not state whether it covers the sensor, the burial hardware or both. No sensor mass is published.
No sensor mass, dimensions or power are publicly specified for the Silicon Audio seismometer, the DAS interrogator or the seismic-while-drilling system in the sources accessed.

The 2025 DAS study (Icarus 445, DOI 10.1016/j.icarus.2025.116848) was read from the OSTI record abstract summary only. The simulant product, interrogator model, channel count, sampling rate and burial depths were not available and are not stated.

The MOONBIT seismic-while-drilling source (ASCE library) returned HTTP 403 and could not be read. Details about MOONBIT geophone placement and results are excluded. The 2015 Poletto et al. paper was read from a bibliographic record abstract, which gives no sensors, simulant or quantitative results.

The LEMS status (hardware complete, not deployed, two seismometers, Goddard clean room pending Artemis assignment) is taken from a NASA article dated 11 August 2026. No LEMS mass, power or dimensions are used in this article, to avoid attributing another instrument's figures to this payload class.
The explanation that sound does not propagate through lunar vacuum, and the general description of DAS interrogation physics, are general background and are not drawn from the sources accessed.
The lunar regolith density, porosity and P-wave velocity values are quoted from the 2019 poster, which cites other literature. The underlying cited works were not checked.
The payload progress ledger was not edited, as instructed. The validator run also writes a .urls.txt file alongside the JSON, which is the existing convention in this folder.
